summary: Gives corrections to RFC 560, the Remote Controlled Transmission and Echoing Telnet option. A fully updated version of the specification was filed in the Protocols Notebook as a separate NIC document.

eli5.summary: A rulebook had a few errors, so this note lists the fixes and says a cleaned-up copy is filed elsewhere.

questions: what is the rcte telnet option
what is the rcte option code
subtitle: Fixes to the Remote Controlled Transmission and Echoing Telnet option from RFC 560.

tldr.problem: RFC 560, which described the RCTE Telnet option, left out the option code, omitted the end of subnegotiation, and was criticised for not letting network I/O and server computation overlap.
tldr.mechanism: This note adds the code RCTE 7, requires IAC SE to end each subnegotiation, and rewrites several sections to make transmission classes guidelines and to tie Break Reset commands to Break characters.
tldr.outcome: A completely updated RCTE specification was journalized for the Protocols Notebook as NIC document 19859.

facts.label: Subnegotiation format
facts.value: IAC SB RCTE, cmd, optional BC and TC bytes, IAC SE

today: The unit metadata lists the status of RFC 581 as Unknown. It updates RFC 560, and the note itself points to a completely updated RCTE specification in the Protocols Notebook.

sections.title: Small Corrections
sections.content:
This note corrects RFC 560. Section 1 was supposed to give the option name and code but left the code out; it should read RCTE 7. Section 2 should end the subnegotiation with the End of Subnegotiation parameter, so the command reads IAC SB RCTE <cmd> [BC1 BC2] [TC1 TC2] IAC SE, and every example should show IAC SE.

The sample scenario in Section 5.D is also to be changed to show the kind of asynchrony of events that can occur. A completely updated version of the specification replaces the original.
sections.eli5: The rulebook forgot to give the option its number and to say how a message ends. These are now added.

sections.title: Transmission and Break Characters
sections.content:
John Davidson's criticism in RFC 563 was that RCTE seemed to stop network I/O and server computation from overlapping. The author agrees and rewrites the definitions to fix it.

  • A Transmission character now only recommends that the Using host send the text accumulated so far, as defined at the moment the character is typed.
  • A Break character requires the Using host to send the text so far and also stops its print/discard action until the Serving host sends another RCTE command.
  • Echoing is suspended after a Break character until the Serving host sends a Break Reset command.
sections.eli5: Before, the rules forced the typing computer to send text at certain keys. Now they are suggestions, except for special stop keys.

sections.title: Buffering and Resets
sections.content:
The note states there are no mandatory transmission constraints: the Using host may send one character at a time, though that wastes RCTE, and the Transmission Classes commands are guidelines. If the buffer fills and further typing would be lost, the user should be notified.

Added rules say the Serving and Using hosts must carefully synchronize Break Class Reset commands with Break characters, so that apart from the start of an interaction the Serving host may only send a Break Reset in response to a Break character. Text should be buffered until the user types a character of the transmission class in force when it is typed. Transmission Class Reset commands may be sent at any time, and on receiving one the Using host should either rescan its buffered text or simply send it as a group, which is simpler. The note also observes that it is possible to define no Break characters except Telnet commands, but calls the mechanism awkward.
sections.eli5: If the typing computer's notepad fills up, it tells the user. The two computers also have to take turns so reset messages match the stop keys.

references.text: RFC 560, Remote Controlled Transmission and Echoing Telnet Option.
